老熊隨筆 · 復盤體

兩條 X 與一道海峽 Two X's and One Strait

一則五年前的 Quora 回答，把女生不念理工歸因於染色體。拆開來看，機制的方向沒錯，量級錯了一個數量級。而東亞那條缺口的真正主因叫滅絕師太效應——一個完全不需要染色體的機制。反證不在遺傳學裡，在地圖上、在作者自己的個人頁上，以及在我家的飯桌上。

老熊　Lao Xiong

摘要　EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

  1. X 連鎖機制的方向對，量級錯一個數量級。男性一條 X 是單次抽樣，女性兩條近似兩次抽樣的平均，變異數減半、標準差縮為 1/√2。但 √2 是天花板，只在「全部變異都掛在 X 上」時成立。X 實際承載約 4–5% 的編碼基因，推得的變異比約 1.01；實測的男女標準差比是 1.05 到 1.15。要用 X 連鎖解釋 1.10，得假設近六成的加成遺傳變異住在 X 上。
  2. 尾端算術成立，但撐不起結論。標準差差 5–10%，到正三、正四個標準差外會放大到 1.6:1 甚至 4:1。問題是當工程師不需要正四個標準差；在真正的門檻附近，預測比例約 1.1:1，離現實的參與率差距差得很遠。
  3. 中央與尾端要用兩把不同的尺。中央極限定理解釋了智商為何近似常態，但它是關於分布中央的陳述。尾端得用極值理論；把常態一路外推到正四個標準差，本身就是未經檢驗的假設。
  4. 跨國數據與染色體無關。日本工程類女性 16%（OECD 平均 26%），韓國工程系大學部約 20%，台灣主修 STEM 28.7%（低於二〇〇五年的 31.4%），美國工程系大學部 22%，大陸數學碩士班逾 60%。所謂「美國博士階段五成居冠」是組成效應——NSF 的實際數字是 S&E 博士女性 41.2%，工程只有約四分之一。
  5. 滅絕師太效應才是東亞那條缺口的主因。上嫁規範預設丈夫學歷、收入、年齡都高於妻子，於是女性學歷越高、合格集合越小，再被年齡梯度削一次。關鍵是：這個代價是預期性的——十八歲選系時就先付了。美國的漏點在博士之後（tenure clock 撞生育年齡），東亞的漏點在博士之前。
  6. 它解釋了數據裡那個翻轉。大陸數學碩士女生逾六成，博士卻掉回 39%。污名掛在「女博士」而非女碩士，所以東亞的曲線不是「女生少進理工」，是女生停在懲罰生效的那一級。

第一節一張截圖

那天收到一張 Quora 的截圖。標題問：為什麼沒有更多女生對 STEM 領域感興趣？署名 Susanna Viljanen 的回答，開頭只有一句——因為那是社交自殺。

往下讀，論證一層一層疊上去。數學很難；難到需要高智商才能真懂；智商相關的基因多半在 X 染色體上；男生只有一條 X，女生有兩條；所以男生的分布比較寬，天才與低能兩端都過度代表，女生則比較集中在平均附近。於是頂端聰明的女生本來就稀少，而且顯得古怪、不合群、沒有社交技巧，容易被排擠。

這個論證的形狀很漂亮。從一條染色體推到一整個產業的人口結構，中間每一步看起來都接得上。漂亮到讓人想把它拆開來看。

第二節兩條 X 的算術

先說結論：這個機制的方向沒錯，量級錯得離譜。

男性只有一條 X，是單次抽樣；女性有兩條，加上隨機去活化，大致相當於兩次抽樣的平均。兩次平均的變異數是單次的一半，標準差因此縮為 1/√2，約 0.707 倍。

但 √2 是天花板，不是估計值。它只在「全部的變異都掛在 X 上」的時候才成立。實際上 X 大約承載 4% 到 5% 的編碼基因。把這個比例代進去，女性的變異數只比男性小 1.5% 上下，變異比大約 1.01。

X 連鎖機制的理論上限　1.41

用真實 X 基因佔比推得的變異比　約 1.01

認知測驗實測的男女標準差比　1.05 – 1.15

要用 X 連鎖解釋 1.10，得假設將近六成的加成遺傳變異都住在 X 染色體上。沒有人會相信這個數字。她拿來當地基的那塊石頭，撐不起她蓋的樓。

尾端的算術倒是站得住。標準差只差 5% 到 10%，到了正三、正四個標準差之外，男女比例會放大到 1.6 比 1 甚至 4 比 1。小小的變異差距在尾端會複利。這一段她說得沒錯——連同「底端也一樣過度代表」那句，雖然用詞粗暴。

問題是當工程師不需要正四個標準差。在真正的門檻附近，預測的比例大約 1.1 比 1。

那個數字離現實中的參與率差距還差得很遠。尾端數學扛不起她壓上去的社會學重量。

第三節為什麼除以二會變成四分之一

中間岔出一個小問題：為什麼兩個同分布隨機變數的算術平均，變異數只剩一半？

因為縮放因子會被平方。變異數的單位是平方單位，乘以二分之一之後其實是乘以四分之一；而兩個獨立變數相加時變異數相加，於是四分之一乘以兩倍的 σ²，剛好是 σ²／2。

直覺版本：平均會讓高低互相抵消。兩次抽樣不太可能同時走極端，所以平均值比任何單獨一次都更靠近中心。標準差縮小的倍率是 √2 ≈ 1.414，不是 2。

但「同分布」必須連「獨立」一起成立。若兩者的相關係數為 ρ，變異數會是 σ²(1+ρ)／2。ρ 等於 1 時完全沒有縮減——因為那等於只抽了一次。

回到染色體：獨立性的假設是父方與母方的 X 攜帶不相關的遺傳值。隨機婚配下還說得過去，但認知特質的選型婚配是有文獻的，配偶相關大約 0.3 到 0.4。ρ 被推高，女性的變異縮減就更小。那個本來就很小的機制，又縮水了一圈。

第四節兩把不同的尺

接著被問到：這是不是中央極限定理在講的事？

一半是。σ²／n 這個結果是純代數，任何 n 都成立，不需要中央極限定理背書。定理真正的貢獻是形狀——即使個別抽樣不是常態，平均之後會趨近常態。所以 n 等於 2 的情形，定理其實沒出力。

有趣的地方在這裡。智商這類特質之所以近似常態，本來就是中央極限定理的功勞：幾千個微小的遺傳與環境貢獻加總起來。但定理講的是分布的中央。而前面整段爭論，把全部的重量都押在正三、正四個標準差之外——恰恰是這把尺最不準的地方。

尾端要用另一把尺：極值理論。Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko 定理說，極大值會收斂到 Gumbel、Fréchet 或 Weibull 家族，不是常態。所以第二節那組尾端比例要加註警語：它假設常態一路成立到正四個標準差，而真實的測驗分布有天花板效應，尾端本來就不乾淨。

在中央用中央極限定理，在尾端用極值理論。爭論的雙方常常拿著中央那把尺去量尾端。

第五節跨過海峽的反證

最後岔到一個實證問題：中國大陸的女生投入 STEM 的比例，是不是真的比美國、台灣、日本、韓國都高？

大致是，但要看是哪個領域、哪個階段。

女性佔比，依地區與領域
地區與領域女性佔比
日本：工程、製造與建築16%
日本：理學、數學與統計27%
韓國：工程系大學部約 20%
台灣：主修 STEM（2014）28.7%
美國：工程系大學部22%
中國大陸：數學碩士班逾 60%

日本是 OECD 的墊底，工程類 16% 對上 OECD 平均的 26%，理學數統類 27% 對上平均的 52%。台灣 2014 年的 28.7%，還低於 2005 年的 31.4%。

但排序會隨階段翻轉，而這裡要先擋掉一個常被引用的數字。流傳的版本說美國博士階段的科技領域女性比例達五成、居各國之冠。那個數字靠不住：美國國家科學基金會自己的統計是，二〇一八年全部科學與工程博士學位中女性佔 41.2%。要衝到五成以上，得把教育、健康科學、人文藝術一起算進籃子裡。

而且 S&E 內部的離散大得驚人。心理學的女性學位比例約七成五，生物科學過半；電腦科學與工程最低。二〇二三年，心理學、健康科學、生物與生醫科學、農業科學、社會科學的博士女性都過半，而電腦與資訊科學、工程、數學與統計、物理科學只有 26% 到 45%。

所以「美國博士階段最高」主要是一個組成效應——美國的籃子裡裝了大量心理學與生命科學，把平均拉了上去。工程對工程，美國博士班女性約四分之一，一點也不高。附帶一提，聯合國教科文組織根本沒有收中國的 STEM 數據，中國自己的定義又比西方寬。跨國比較在這一層已經不太乾淨。

  • 性別平等悖論。越富裕、性別越平等的國家，女性 STEM 比例反而越低。希臘、冰島、波蘭超過 40%，瑞士與智利不到 25%，絕對差距最大的是芬蘭、德國、瑞典。諷刺的是，那篇 Quora 的作者正是芬蘭人。
  • 社會主義遺產。「婦女能頂半邊天」不只是口號。蘇聯式的工科教育加上全面勞動動員，留下了耐久的規範。同樣的圖案出現在俄羅斯、白俄羅斯與中亞。
  • 一胎化。城市裡的獨生女，拿到了本來要分給兒子的全部教育投資。台灣、日本、韓國沒有對應的政策。
  • 高考。分數決定分發，程序機械而匿名。台灣的研究正好佐證：在申請 STEM 科系的條件下，女性錄取率不低於條件相當的男性——缺口幾乎全部發生在「誰去申請」這一步。
  • 分流時間。文理分科在大陸發生得比較晚、也比較不可逆。台灣的研究同樣把女性 STEM 參與率的上升，連到高中階段分流的延後。

該加的但書：這個優勢在畢業之後大致蒸發。中國學術界的資深階層以男性壓倒多數，招聘廣告寫「男性優先」在被整頓之前是常態。大陸把女生變成 STEM 畢業生做得不錯，變成 STEM 領導者做得很差——那是管線上另一個漏點，不是沒有漏點。

第六節滅絕師太：一個不需要染色體的機制

第五節列的那幾條理由都是制度性的，但漏了一條最要命的。它在東亞有個現成的名字：滅絕師太效應。

指的是讀到博士的女人不好嫁，所以多數女生不敢冒這個險。

底下的機制叫上嫁規範。東亞婚配長期預設丈夫的學歷、收入、年齡都高於妻子；台灣與東亞其他地區一樣，有很強的教育上嫁傳統——男性娶學歷低於自己的女性。當女性的教育與職位提升，可匹配的對象池必然縮小：符合「地位相當」條件的男性數量本身就減少了。

博士這一級之所以是斷點，純粹是算術。女博士的合格集合被兩件事同時削：一是只剩學歷相當或更高的男性，二是那批男性在同一個市場裡傾向找更年輕的。三十歲拿到學位的人，同時面對一個被規範限制住、又正在被年齡梯度抽走的池子。

這不是她找不到。是合格的集合被規範定義掉了。

而且規範必須雙方都持有才成立：男方不願娶學歷更高的，女方也不願嫁學歷更低的。那是一個協調均衡，不是一種性格。

漏點的位置不一樣

美國的漏點在博士之後：六年的 tenure clock 壓在三十到三十六歲，博士後合約短、要搬家，聯邦沒有給薪育嬰假。那是時程表製造出來的二選一。

東亞的漏點在博士之前，而且是預期性的。十八歲選系的女生，是在替十二年後的婚配市場先付代價。

這一點反而比第二節的變異數算術更徹底地打掉那篇 Quora 的論證。上嫁規範可以在男女智力分布完全相同的前提下，精準產生我們看到的每一個數字。不需要染色體，一條都不需要。

它解釋了那個翻轉

大陸的數學碩士班女生超過六成，博士階段卻掉回三成九。台灣、日本、韓國是同一個形狀。

因為污名掛在「女博士」那三個字上，不掛在女碩士。東亞的曲線不是「女生比較少進理工」，而是女生停在懲罰開始生效的那一級。碩士安全，博士不安全，於是就停在碩士。

兩個但書

一，懲罰在弱化，但信念還在。日本的研究顯示，女性婚配的負教育梯度到二〇〇五年已經消失，二〇〇九年後甚至轉正。實際的懲罰在鬆動，但十八歲時所依據的預期仍然是舊的。決策發生在信念上，不發生在統計上。

二，這是個會移動的東西。新加坡因為女性大學畢業率高於男性，同一套規範撞上不同的供給，結果變成大量高學歷女性與低學歷男性同時單身。規範會隨供給、政策與世代改變。

染色體不會。

第七節家裡的反例

該說清楚這篇文章是怎麼開始的。

前面那四個問題——染色體、變異數、兩把尺、跨國比例——看起來像一串技術性的好奇心。其實不是。它們是同一個問題的四種問法，而那個問題我早就有答案了，只是想看看數據會不會同意。

田總來自中國大陸。一九八二年高考，上海考區第五名，進上海交通大學，一九八六屆。畢業之後一路做工程，三十多年沒離開過這一行，現在在一家工程顧問公司。

把這個數字放回第四節的尺上：一整個上海考區的第五名。那是分布最右邊的那一小撮裡，再往右數到第五個。而那一年的排名是純分數決定的，考卷上不寫性別。

她也不是什麼「稀有的例外」——她那一屆的女生本來就多。第五節列的那幾條理由，蘇聯式的工科教育、勞動動員、分數決定分發、分流時間晚，講的正是她那一代人走過的路。

而那篇 Quora 答案說，這樣的女生罕見、古怪、沒有社交能力、會被排擠。

我跟這位「罕見的古怪例外」一起吃了幾十年的晚飯。

所以第五節那個問題——大陸的女生是不是真的比較多念理工——對我從來不是研究題目。那是把手上唯一的樣本，拿去對母體查核一遍。數據同意了。

至於這篇文章的標題：一道海峽的兩邊，一邊是台大，一邊是上海交大。跨海峽比較對我不是題材，是家裡的事。

第八節尾聲

回頭看那張截圖。然後往上拉，看作者的個人頁。

也就是說：寫下「女生的分布比較窄、所以理工系裡女生少」的人，自己是芬蘭最好的理工大學畢業的。她站在自己論證所預測的那個稀有位置上，而且不只站著——她在那裡寫了兩萬一千則答案，累積三億四千萬次閱讀。

這不是抓語病。這是整篇文章的解釋。那篇答案讀起來像是在報導別人，其實是一份自述，被推廣成了一條定律。「我覺得數學很難」變成「數學很難」；「我被排擠」變成「聰明的女生會被排擠」；「我是例外」變成「例外很罕見，因為染色體」。

用我這行的話講：她拿單一樣本建了一個模型，然後把它外推到整個母體，而且沒有給信賴區間。

駁倒染色體論證最乾淨的證據，不在遺傳學裡，在地圖和日曆裡。芬蘭女性與中國女性的染色體一模一樣。台灣女性主修 STEM 的比例在九年之內從 31.4% 掉到 28.7%。

染色體不會在九年之內改變，也不會渡過台灣海峽。

會隨政策、世代與國界移動的那個東西，不管它是什麼，都不是遺傳學能解釋的。

那位作者在文末寫，自己其實一開始就因為溝通距離而社交性死亡了。把自己的孤立解釋成染色體宿命，等於是把一件很可能可以改變的事，交給一個無法反駁的機制去承接。那不是統計問題，但那大概才是整篇答案真正在寫的東西。

而她的論證之所以站不住，最後並不是因為變異比是 1.01 而不是 1.15。

是因為我可以指著一個人。

一九八二 · 上海考區第五名分布最右端的那一小撮，再往右數到第五個。純分數決定，考卷不寫性別。

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

  1. The X-linked mechanism points the right way and is wrong by an order of magnitude. One X is a single draw; two X's with random inactivation behave like the average of two, halving the variance and shrinking the standard deviation by 1/√2. But √2 is a ceiling, true only if all variance sat on the X. The X carries roughly 4–5% of coding genes, implying a variance ratio near 1.01, against an observed male/female SD ratio of 1.05–1.15. Explaining 1.10 by X-linkage would require nearly 60% of additive genetic variance to live on one chromosome.
  2. The tail arithmetic is sound but cannot carry the conclusion. A 5–10% SD gap widens to 1.6:1 or 4:1 past three or four standard deviations. But engineering does not require four standard deviations; at the real threshold the predicted ratio is about 1.1:1, nowhere near observed participation gaps.
  3. The centre and the tails need different rulers. The central limit theorem explains why IQ-like traits are approximately normal, but it is a statement about the centre. Tails need extreme value theory; extrapolating normality out to +4 SD is itself an untested assumption.
  4. The cross-national data has nothing to do with chromosomes. Japan: 16% women in engineering against an OECD average of 26%. Korea: about 20% of undergraduate engineering. Taiwan: 28.7% of STEM majors, down from 31.4% in 2005. US: 22% of undergraduate engineering. Mainland China: over 60% of mathematics master's students. The widely quoted "US leads with just over half of S&T doctorates" is a composition effect — NSF's actual figure is 41.2% of S&E doctorates, and about a quarter in engineering.
  5. The marriage penalty is the main driver of the East Asian gap. The hypergamy norm assumes the husband outranks the wife in education, income, and age, so a woman's eligible set shrinks as her credentials rise, then shrinks again under the age gradient. Crucially the cost is anticipatory — paid at eighteen, when the major is chosen. America's leak comes after the doctorate (tenure clock against childbearing years); East Asia's comes before it.
  6. It explains the flip in the data. Mainland mathematics master's programmes are over 60% women, yet the doctoral share falls to 39%. The stigma attaches to the doctorate, not the master's. The East Asian curve is not "fewer women entering STEM" but women stopping exactly where the penalty begins.

PART ONEThe Screenshot

A Quora screenshot arrived one afternoon. The question asked why more girls aren't interested in STEM. The answer, signed Susanna Viljanen, opened with a single line: because it is social suicide.

The argument stacked up layer by layer. Mathematics is hard. Hard enough that really understanding it requires high intelligence. Most intelligence-related genes sit on the X chromosome. Boys have one X, girls have two. Therefore the male distribution is wider, over-represented at both the genius end and the bottom, while girls cluster nearer the average. So brilliant girls are rare to begin with, and the few who exist look weird, unsociable, and get excluded.

It is a handsome argument. It runs from one chromosome to the demographics of an entire industry, and every joint looks like it fits. Handsome enough to make you want to take it apart.

↑ Back to contents

PART TWOThe Arithmetic of Two X's

The short version: the direction of the mechanism is right, and the magnitude is wrong by an order of magnitude.

A male is hemizygous — one X, a single draw. A female has two, and with random inactivation her value behaves roughly like the average of two draws. The variance of an average of two is half that of one draw, so female standard deviation shrinks by a factor of 1/√2, about 0.707.

But √2 is the ceiling, not the estimate. It holds only if every scrap of variance sat on the X. In reality the X carries something like 4–5% of coding genes. Put that number in and female variance comes out around 1.5% below male — a variance ratio near 1.01.

Theoretical ceiling of the X-linked mechanism　1.41

Ratio implied by the real X gene share　about 1.01

Observed male/female SD ratio on cognitive tests　1.05 – 1.15

To get 1.10 out of X-linkage you would need close to 60% of all additive genetic variance living on the X chromosome. Nobody believes that number. The stone she used for a foundation cannot hold the building she put on it.

The tail arithmetic, on the other hand, is sound. A standard deviation gap of only 5–10% widens to ratios of 1.6-to-1 or even 4-to-1 once you pass three or four standard deviations out. Small variance differences compound in the tails. She has that part right — including the point that the same over-representation appears at the bottom, crudely as she words it.

The trouble is that becoming an engineer does not require four standard deviations. At the real threshold, the predicted ratio is roughly 1.1 to 1.

That is nowhere near the participation gaps we actually observe. The tail mathematics cannot carry the sociological load she piles onto it.

↑ Back to contents

PART THREEWhy Halving Becomes Quartering

A smaller question branched off midway: why does the arithmetic mean of two identically distributed variables have only half the variance?

Because the scaling factor gets squared. Variance lives in squared units, so multiplying by one half is really multiplying by one quarter; and variances of independent variables add, so one quarter times two σ² lands exactly on σ²/2.

The intuition: averaging lets highs and lows cancel. Two draws rarely go extreme together, so the average sits closer to the centre than either one alone. The standard deviation shrinks by √2 ≈ 1.414, not by 2.

But "identically distributed" has to come with "independent." If the correlation is ρ, the variance is σ²(1+ρ)/2. At ρ = 1 there is no reduction at all, because you effectively drew once.

Back to the chromosomes. Independence here means the maternal and paternal X carry uncorrelated genetic values. Fine under random mating — but assortative mating for cognitive traits is well documented, with spousal correlations around 0.3 to 0.4. That pushes ρ up and shrinks the female variance reduction further. A mechanism that was already tiny gets smaller still.

↑ Back to contents

PART FOURTwo Different Rulers

Then came the question: is this what the central limit theorem is about?

Half of it. The σ²/n result is pure algebra, true for any n, requiring no theorem at all. What the CLT actually contributes is shape — the average converges toward normal even when the individual draws are not. For the n = 2 case, the theorem does no work.

Here is the interesting part. The CLT is the reason IQ-like traits are approximately normal in the first place: thousands of small genetic and environmental contributions summing together. But the theorem is a statement about the centre of a distribution. And the whole preceding argument put all its weight three and four standard deviations out — precisely where that ruler is least accurate.

The tails need a different instrument: extreme value theory. Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko says maxima converge to the Gumbel, Fréchet, or Weibull families, not to a normal. So the tail ratios in Part Two deserve a health warning: they assume exact normality all the way to +4 SD, and real test distributions have ceiling effects and messy tails.

Use the CLT at the centre and extreme value theory at the tails. Both sides of this argument habitually measure the tails with the ruler built for the middle.

↑ Back to contents

PART FIVEThe Counter-Evidence Across the Strait

The last turn was empirical: are more women in mainland China actually going into STEM than in the US, Taiwan, Japan, or Korea?

Broadly yes — but it depends which field and which stage.

Female share, by place and field
Place and fieldFemale share
Japan: engineering, manufacturing, construction16%
Japan: science, mathematics, statistics27%
South Korea: undergraduate engineering~20%
Taiwan: STEM majors (2014)28.7%
United States: undergraduate engineering22%
Mainland China: mathematics master'sover 60%

Japan sits at the bottom of the OECD: 16% against an OECD average of 26% in engineering, 27% against 52% in science and mathematics. Taiwan's 28.7% in 2014 was lower than its own 31.4% in 2005.

The ranking flips by stage — but one widely circulated figure has to be blocked first. The version in circulation says American women take just over half of all doctorates in science and technology, the highest of any country. That number does not hold up. The National Science Foundation's own count is that women earned 41.2% of all science and engineering doctorates in 2018. Getting above half requires putting education, health sciences, and the humanities into the same basket.

And the spread inside S&E is enormous. Women take about three quarters of psychology degrees and more than half in the biological sciences; computer science and engineering are the lowest. In 2023, women earned more than half of the doctorates in psychology, health sciences, biological and biomedical sciences, agricultural sciences, and the social sciences, but only 26% to 45% in computer and information sciences, engineering, mathematics and statistics, and the physical sciences.

So the American lead at doctoral level is mostly a composition effect: the American basket is full of psychology and life science, which pulls the average up. Engineering against engineering, American doctoral programmes are about one quarter women, which is not high at all. Note also that UNESCO publishes no STEM figures for China, and China's own definition of the category runs broader than Western ones. Cross-national comparison is already unclean at this level.

  • The gender-equality paradox. Richer and more gender-egalitarian countries have lower female STEM shares. Greece, Iceland, and Poland exceed 40%; Switzerland and Chile fall below 25%; the widest absolute gaps include Finland, Germany, and Sweden. The irony is that the Quora author is Finnish.
  • Socialist legacy. 婦女能頂半邊天 was never only a slogan. Soviet-model polytechnic education plus mass labour mobilisation left a durable norm. The same pattern shows in Russia, Belarus, and Central Asia.
  • The one-child policy. An urban only-daughter received the full educational investment that would otherwise have been split with a son. Taiwan, Japan, and Korea had no equivalent.
  • The gaokao. Scores determine placement, mechanically and anonymously. Taiwanese research supports the point from the other side: conditional on applying to a STEM programme, women are admitted at least as often as comparable men — the gap sits almost entirely in who applies.
  • Timing of streaming. The arts/science split happens later and less irreversibly on the mainland. Taiwanese work likewise ties rising female STEM participation to delayed streaming at upper secondary level.

The caveat that matters: the advantage largely evaporates after graduation. Senior Chinese academic ranks are overwhelmingly male, and job advertisements reading 男性優先 were routine until recent crackdowns. The mainland converts girls into STEM graduates well and into STEM leaders poorly — a different leak in the pipeline, not the absence of one.

PART SIXThe Marriage Penalty: A Mechanism That Needs No Chromosome

The reasons in Part Five are all institutional, but they leave out the one that bites hardest. In East Asia it already has a name — the 滅絕師太 effect, after the fierce celibate abbess in the martial-arts novels.

It means this: a woman who takes a doctorate becomes hard to marry, so most women do not risk it.

The mechanism underneath is the hypergamy norm. East Asian marriage has long assumed that the husband outranks the wife in education, income, and age. Taiwan, like the rest of the region, has a strong tradition of educational hypergamy — men marrying women with less education than themselves. As women's education and occupational standing rise, the pool of eligible partners necessarily shrinks, because the number of men meeting the "adequate status" condition falls.

The doctorate is the breaking point for a purely arithmetic reason. A woman's eligible set gets cut twice: once down to men of equal or higher credentials, and again by the fact that those men, in the same market, tend to look younger. A woman finishing at thirty faces a pool that is both restricted by the norm and being drained by the age gradient.

It is not that she cannot find anyone. It is that the eligible set has been defined away by a norm.

And the norm requires both sides to hold it: men unwilling to marry up, women unwilling to marry down. That is a coordination equilibrium, not a personality type.

The leak sits in a different place

The American leak comes after the doctorate: a six-year tenure clock landing squarely on ages thirty to thirty-six, short postdoc contracts that require moving, and no federal paid parental leave. That is a dilemma manufactured by a schedule.

The East Asian leak comes before the doctorate, and it is anticipatory. An eighteen-year-old choosing her major is pre-paying a cost in a marriage market twelve years away.

This demolishes the Quora argument more completely than the variance arithmetic in Part Two ever could. The hypergamy norm can produce every number we observe while male and female ability distributions remain exactly identical. No chromosome required. Not one.

It explains the flip

Mainland mathematics master's programmes are over 60% women, yet the doctoral share falls back to 39%. Taiwan, Japan, and Korea show the same shape.

Because the stigma attaches to the word "doctorate," not to the master's. The East Asian curve is not "fewer women entering STEM." It is women stopping at exactly the level where the penalty begins. The master's is safe; the doctorate is not; so they stop at the master's.

Two caveats

First, the penalty is weakening but the belief is not. Japanese research finds that the negative educational gradient in women's marriage had disappeared by 2005 and turned positive by 2009. The actual penalty is loosening, but the expectation an eighteen-year-old acts on is still the old one. The decision runs on belief, not on the statistics.

Second, this thing moves. In Singapore, where women now graduate from university at higher rates than men, the same norm meets a different supply and produces large numbers of highly educated women and less educated men single at the same time. Norms shift with supply, policy, and generation.

Chromosomes do not.

PART SEVENThe Counterexample at Home

It is worth saying plainly how this piece started.

The four questions above — chromosomes, variance, the two rulers, the cross-national shares — look like a string of technical curiosity. They are not. They are four ways of asking the same question, and I already had the answer. I only wanted to see whether the data would agree.

田總 is from mainland China. In the 1982 gaokao she placed fifth in the entire Shanghai examination district, went to Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and graduated in 1986. She went straight into engineering and has stayed in it for more than thirty years; she works at an engineering consulting firm now.

Put that number back on the ruler from Part Four: fifth in all of Shanghai. That is the far right edge of the distribution, and then four more places to the right. The ranking was decided by score alone. The exam paper does not record sex.

Nor is she a rare exception — her cohort had plenty of women in it. The reasons listed in Part Five, the Soviet-model polytechnic education, the labour mobilisation, placement by score, the late streaming, describe the road her generation actually walked.

The Quora answer says women like that are rare, weird, socially unskilled, and get excluded.

I have been eating dinner with this rare, weird exception for several decades.

So the question in Part Five — whether mainland women really do go into STEM more often — was never a research topic for me. It was checking my single sample against the population. The data agreed.

As for the title of this piece: one side of the strait is NTU, the other is Shanghai Jiao Tong. The cross-strait comparison is not subject matter. It is the household.

PART EIGHTCoda

Back to the screenshot. Then scroll up, to the author's own profile.

So: the person who wrote that the female distribution is narrower, and that this is why engineering schools are short of women, is herself a graduate of Finland's leading technical university. She occupies the rare position her own argument predicts — and not quietly. She has written twenty-one thousand answers from it, read three hundred and forty million times.

This is not a gotcha. It is the explanation of the piece. The answer reads like a report about other people; it is a self-description promoted to a law. "I found mathematics hard" becomes "mathematics is hard." "I was excluded" becomes "bright girls are excluded." "I am the exception" becomes "exceptions are rare, because of chromosomes."

In the language of my old trade: she built a model on a single sample, extrapolated it to the whole population, and reported no confidence interval.

The cleanest refutation of the chromosome argument is not in genetics. It is on the map and on the calendar. Finnish women and Chinese women have identical chromosomes. Taiwan's female STEM share fell from 31.4% to 28.7% in nine years.

Chromosomes do not change in nine years, and they do not cross the Taiwan Strait.

Whatever moves with policy, cohort, and border — whatever it is — genetics cannot explain it.

At the end of her answer, the author writes that she was socially dead from the start anyway, because of the communication range. Explaining your own isolation as chromosomal destiny hands something that was probably changeable over to a mechanism nobody can argue with. That is not a statistics problem, but it is probably what the answer was really about.

And in the end her argument does not fail because the variance ratio is 1.01 rather than 1.15.

It fails because I can point at a person.
